title: Ko v. Li — show-cause order for contempt in the face of the court over apparent AI-fabricated citations
author: Frederick L. Myers

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The court squarely supports technology-neutral human accountability: lawyers must independently review AI-assisted materials, verify cited authorities, and remain responsible for misleading submissions. Its emphasis on suspicious citations, incomplete facts, and counsel’s failure to explain or correct the filing also aligns with targeting deficient inquiry and post-discovery conduct rather than AI use itself.

kp.k: Court identifies nonexistent authorities and a reversed case holding
kp.d: Myers J identified concrete defects in applicant counsel Jisuh Lee’s April 25, 2025 factum, relied upon at the May 1 hearing. Citations to Alam v. Shah and Meschino Estate linked to unrelated commercial real estate and wrongful dismissal decisions; the DaCosta link returned a page-not-found error. The judge could not locate those three cited cases across CanLII, Westlaw, Quicklaw or Google. A fourth authority, Johnson v. Lanka, existed but dismissed the trustee-removal applications, contrary to counsel’s representation that a trustee had been removed. These are documented citation and characterization problems, not measured AI error rates.
qs: When the hyperlinks did not take me to the cases cited, I searched the CanLII website to try to find the cases. I could not find them.
In fact, the opposite is true. The court did not remove the estate trustees.
But I have also determined that the three unknown cases discussed above are also not found on any of Westlaw, Quicklaw, or Google.

kp.k: AI involvement remains suspected, not established
kp.d: The judge considered the defects similar to generative-AI hallucination incidents and suggested that the factum might have been AI-generated without adequate checking. When asked about AI preparation, Lee said her office did not usually use it and that she would need to check with her clerk. The endorsement expressly leaves open alternative explanations, including incorrect hyperlinks and misunderstanding Johnson; it does not establish that AI produced these errors.
qs: She told me that her office does not usually do so but that she would have to check with her clerk.
I do not know the full facts yet.
Perhaps wrong hyperlinks were given for cases.
Perhaps AI was not used to create the factum and these are not examples of hallucinations. Perhaps counsel misunderstood Johnson.

kp.k: Lawyers retain responsibility for human verification and staff supervision
kp.d: Myers J states that lawyers must use technology competently, supervise staff, review materials prepared for signature, and ensure human review of generative-AI materials. Verification extends beyond confirming that a case exists: counsel must read authorities and ensure that they support the propositions submitted. These obligations are presented as lawyers’ existing duties to courts, clients and the administration of justice, rather than responsibilities displaced by technological or staff assistance.
qs: It is the lawyer’s duty to use technology, conduct legal research, and prepare court documents competently.
It is the lawyer’s duty to supervise staff and review material prepared for her signature.
It is the lawyer’s duty to ensure human review of materials prepared by non-human technology such as generative artificial intelligence.
It should go without saying that it is the lawyer’s duty to read cases before submitting them to a court as precedential authorities.
It is the litigation lawyer’s most fundamental duty not to mislead the court.

kp.k: Fabricated citations threaten the administration of justice
kp.d: The endorsement quotes Masuhara J in Zhang v Chen, 2024 BCSC 285, characterizing fake citations as abuse of process, equivalent to false statements, and capable of causing miscarriages of justice. Myers J endorses a firm response regardless of whether technology caused the error and describes the sudden advent of AI as making the issue particularly important. The miscarriage-of-justice warning is attributed to the cited judgment, not reported as an outcome established in Ko v. Li.
qs: Citing fake cases in court filings and other materials handed up to the court is an abuse of process and is tantamount to making a false statement to the court. Unchecked, it can lead to a miscarriage of justice.
The court must quickly and firmly make clear that, regardless of technology, lawyers cannot rely on non-existent authorities or cases that say the opposite of what is submitted.
With the sudden advent of AI, this has quickly become a very important issue.

kp.k: Reliance in court prompts possible contempt, not established guilt
kp.d: Myers J contrasts Zhang, where counsel corrected the mistake before the hearing, apologized and withdrew the factum, with Lee’s oral reliance on two suspicious cases and absence of subsequent explanation or correction by the time of this endorsement. He orders Lee to show cause why she should not be cited for contempt in the face of the court, while expressly preserving the presumption of innocence and an opportunity to explain. The May 6, 2025 endorsement initiates scrutiny of possible professional breaches; it does not find contempt or impose a final sanction.
qs: In that case, the lawyer caught her mistake before the hearing, apologized to all, and withdrew her factum. Here, counsel actively relied on two of the suspicious cases as part of her submissions in open court.
Ms. Lee may have committed grave breaches of her duties that may amount to contempt in the face of the court.
I order Ms. Lee to show cause why she should not be cited for contempt.
Despite the traditional wording of this notice, Ms. Lee is protected by the presumption of innocence and other procedural rights as discussed by the Court of Appeal in Cohn.
She will have a fair opportunity to submit evidence to explain what happened if she wishes to do so.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Justice F. L. Myers identifies fabricated legal citations as a risk of generative-AI drafting and states that lawyers must verify AI-prepared materials before relying on them in court.
pts.d: Myers presents AI hallucinations as an existing litigation problem, not a forecast about employment or legal markets. He suggests that the applicant’s factum may have been AI-generated and submitted without checking whether its authorities existed or supported its propositions. He states that technological assistance does not displace lawyers’ duties of competent research, staff supervision, human review and accurate representation of the law. The apparent failures here prompted a show-cause order for possible contempt, not a finding that AI was used or that contempt occurred.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of Myers’s examination of the filed factum, searches for its authorities, counsel’s responses at the hearing, and references to other judicial cases—not model-performance measurements.
pts.d: Two hyperlinks for purported authorities led to unrelated decisions, another returned a missing-page error, and a real trustee-removal decision was described as reaching the opposite of its actual result. Myers could not locate three purported cases on CanLII, Westlaw, Quicklaw or Google. Counsel could not supply the cases at the hearing and said she would need to check with her clerk about AI use. Myers also cites Zhang v Chen and Benjamin v Costco as judicial examples of similar problems. The warning that fake citations can cause a miscarriage of justice is explicitly quoted from Masuhara J. in Zhang, rather than presented as original language by Myers. These are case-based observations; the endorsement supplies no measured hallucination rate or proof of AI authorship in this instance.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The endorsement treats hallucinated authorities as an urgent present issue in May 2025, while expressly reserving judgment about AI use and counsel’s culpability.
pts.d: The factum was dated April 25, 2025; counsel relied on suspicious authorities at the May 1 hearing; the endorsement was released May 6. Myers’s verification requirement applies before filing and courtroom reliance. He acknowledges possible alternative explanations, including incorrect hyperlinks, no AI involvement and misunderstanding of the real decision. Counsel retains the presumption of innocence and an opportunity to explain. No longer-term prediction is offered.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are litigation lawyers and their staff, clients, courts and the administration of justice.
pts.d: Lawyers remain responsible for reading and checking authorities, supervising staff and reviewing material submitted under their signatures; failures may expose them to contempt proceedings. In this case the court undertook additional searches and initiated a separate proceeding concerning counsel’s conduct. Clients and the justice system are the beneficiaries of the duties Myers identifies. He does not quantify client harm, costs, productivity effects or market-wide consequences, and the substantive motion was addressed separately from the suspected AI issue.
